newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Martin seen beating his deficit targets.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Martin seen beating his deficit targets.

text.p: Canadian Finance Minister Paul Martin will deliver more good fiscal news in his autumn budget update on Wednesday, possibly undershooting his deficit target for fiscal 1995/96 by more than C$4.5 billion and setting the stage for more reductions, analysts said on Tuesday.

But Canada's financial markets, which have rallied in recent weeks amid positive economic data and interest rate declines, will be looking for signs that tax cuts are in the offing, before extending recent gains.
"I think the market will be watching very closely to see any hints of tax cuts. He (Martin) will be very closely scrutinized," said Canada Trust chief economist Patti Croft.
On Wednesday, Martin will report the final figures for his 1995/96 (April-March) budget, widely seen as the first credible step toward cutting Canada's large deficit.

He has said repeatedly that he would undershoot his C$32.7 billion deficit target and report a deficit of under C$30 billion. Most of that had been expected to come from the C$2.5 billion contingency reserve, which has been unused.
Analysts said Martin could do even better, reporting a deficit as low as C$28 to C$29 billion for 1995/96.

"I expect him to announce that because of the windfall of lower than expected interest rates, he will better his target by a matter of several billion dollars and that he is on track for taking (the deficit) down to one percent of GDP by 1998/99," Croft said.
In his last budget, delivered in March, Martin pledged to cut the deficit to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1996/97 and to 2.0 percent of GDP in 1997/98.
Cutting the deficit to 1.0 percent of GDP in 1998/99 would be the logical next step, followed by a balanced budget by the year 2000, analysts said.
But Martin has resisted setting a date for balancing the budget and is unlikely to give one on Wednesday. Instead, he has preferred to set a series of two-year rolling targets for his deficit cuts.

He is also unlikely to lower his deficit target for the current fiscal year from the C$24.3 billion projected in the March budget. His C$17 billion deficit target for 1997/98 would also remain unchanged, analysts said.
"I don't expect him to officially change his forecasts. If he does, that's very, very bullish news," said Douglas Porter, senior economist at Nesbitt Burns.
Porter said a 1996/97 deficit of C$21 billion was "quite achievable."
"And that is a conservative estimate. It may well be better than that," he said.
But after two straight years of deficit slashing, Martin is coming under pressure to reward Canadians with some form of tax relief in the near future.
The call for tax cuts is being sounded by some economists, opposition party politicians and even members of the ruling Liberal Party, ahead of a likely election next year.

Last week, Ernie Eves, finance minister for Ontario, Canada's richest province, said he would not discuss a plan to rescue the Canada Pension Plan until he saw a reduction in unemployment insurance premiums, effectively a business tax cut.
Martin has resisted straying from his deficit reduction path and economists said any tax cuts could cause concern in financial markets.
"The thing to keep in mind is that it was just a year and a half ago that (Canada's debt ratings) were downgraded and many saw us on the brink of a full blown fiscal crisis," said Nesbitt's Porter.
-- Reuters Ottawa Bureau 613-235-6745
